NFL Teasers: Why Crossing 3 and 7 Is the Classic Play

Published August 22, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

A teaser is one of the few bet types in football where the sportsbook is openly handing you a discount — you get to move the spread in your favor on every leg of the ticket, in exchange for worse odds than a straight parlay would pay. Most of the time that trade isn't worth making. But there's one specific, widely taught version of it, the 6-point teaser that moves a spread across both 3 and 7, where the math genuinely tilts back toward the bettor. Understanding why that particular shape works, and why most other teasers don't, is the whole point of learning this bet.

  2. Why 3 and 7 dominate NFL scoring margins

What a teaser actually does to your spread

A teaser lets you shift the point spread (and sometimes the total) on every leg of a multi-team bet by a fixed number of points, standardized at most US sportsbooks in 6, 6.5, or 7-point increments for NFL games. In exchange, all legs still have to hit for the ticket to cash, exactly like a parlay, but the payout is far lower than a standard parlay of the same size because you've made every leg meaningfully easier to win. If a team is favored by 3, a 6-point teaser turns that into a 9-point cushion; if an underdog is getting 3, the same teaser turns it into 9 points of insurance. You're not picking better teams — you're buying room on lines you already liked.

The catch is that teasers require at least two legs, exactly like parlays, and every leg still has to win. A 6-point teaser doesn't reduce risk to zero, it reduces the size of the swing you're exposed to on each individual game — which only matters if the extra points you're buying actually cross a number that stops close games from beating you.

Why 3 and 7 dominate NFL scoring margins

NFL games end with a final margin of exactly 3 points (a single field goal) or exactly 7 points (a touchdown with the extra point) far more often than any other margin, because touchdowns and field goals are the two scoring plays that decide close games. That clustering is why sportsbooks treat 3 and 7 as "key numbers" — a half-point of spread movement across either of them is worth dramatically more than a half-point of movement anywhere else on the number line, say between 8.5 and 9. A 6-point teaser is specifically sized to be able to move a typical short favorite or short underdog spread across both 3 and 7 in a single trade, which is exactly why the number 6 became the industry standard rather than something smaller or larger.

A worked example: turning two coin-flip spreads into a teaser

Say you like two teams as 2.5-point favorites this week — close to a coin flip against the spread on their own. Tease each one down 6 points and each becomes a 3.5-point favorite instead, meaning your team can now lose the game outright by a field goal and you still win the bet, or win outright and you still win the bet. You've bought your way past the single most common losing margin in the sport on both legs at once. Compare that to teasing a team from 9.5 down to 3.5 — you've crossed 7, which is valuable, but you've spent the same 6 points crossing only one key number instead of two, which is a meaningfully worse trade even though the final line number looks similar.

Original spreadAfter a 6-point teaseKey numbers crossed
-2.5 (favorite)+3.5Both 3 and 7 (this is the classic play)
+2.5 (underdog)+8.5Both 3 and 7
-9.5 (favorite)-3.5Only 7
-1.5 (favorite)+4.5Only 3

This is the reason teaser strategy content always circles back to the same instruction: look for favorites in the 1.5-to-2.5-point range and underdogs in the same range, since those are the specific starting spreads a standard 6-point tease carries across both key numbers at once. A favorite already sitting at -8 or a team getting 9.5 points doesn't offer the same double crossing, and the tease is worth much less even though it still "moves the line."

The "Wong teaser": crossing both numbers on both legs

The strategy above has a name in betting circles — a "Wong teaser," after blackjack author Stanford Wong, who popularized the idea of only teasing favorites of 1.5 to 2.5 points and underdogs of 1.5 to 2.5 points, specifically because those are the ranges where a standard 6-point tease crosses both 3 and 7. The logic doesn't require picking winning teams in any traditional sense — it's a mechanical rule based entirely on where a spread sits before the tease, which is part of why it's one of the few "systems" in sports betting with a real mathematical basis rather than a gut read on matchups.

It's worth being honest about the limits here too: this edge, where it exists at all, is thin, and sportsbooks have adjusted over the years by widening teaser odds and, in some cases, restricting or repricing teasers that fall squarely into the Wong range. It's a legitimate piece of betting theory, not a guaranteed profit engine.

Why the payout shrinks as legs increase

Every point of margin you buy costs you in the payout odds, and that cost compounds as you add teams. A two-team, 6-point NFL teaser commonly pays close to even money or slightly worse at major sportsbooks, since you're only slightly favored on two now-easier legs. Add a third team and the odds jump to a moderate underdog price, because now three independent events all have to land instead of two. By five or six teams, standard 6-point teaser payouts stretch out considerably, similar in shape to how parlay payouts grow with each added leg, just starting from worse odds because each leg was made easier to hit.

Teams teasedTypical payout shape (6-point NFL teaser)
2 teamsNear even money, sometimes a slight underdog price
3 teamsModerate underdog payout, roughly in line with a 3-team even-money parlay
4 teamsNoticeably higher payout, but four independent legs must all hit
5-6 teamsLong-shot payout territory — exact odds vary meaningfully by sportsbook

Exact numbers vary by operator and change over time, so treat that table as a shape, not a quote — always check the specific odds a sportsbook is offering on its teaser card before betting, since two books can price the same size teaser noticeably differently.

Takeaway: A 6-point teaser is a good trade when it moves a short favorite or short underdog across both 3 and 7 at once — that's the entire strategic idea in one sentence. Outside of that specific window, you're usually just accepting worse odds for a smaller edge than you think you're buying.

Where teasers stop making sense

The most common teaser mistake is treating any point movement as valuable, rather than checking whether the points actually cross 3 or 7. Teasing a 10-point favorite down to 4 still leaves you exposed to the second-most-common margin in football, and teasing a total that was never close to a key total number (football totals cluster differently than spreads, with less concentration at any single number) often buys very little real protection. Piling on extra teams for a bigger payout is another frequent error — every additional leg is another independent game that has to break your way, and the false comfort of "the points make this safe" can obscure how much correlation-free risk is still sitting on a five- or six-team ticket. For a broader look at how NFL spreads and totals are built in the first place, see our NFL betting guide, and for how teasers compare to standard multi-leg bets generally, see our guide on common bet types.

Frequently asked questions

What's the actual difference between a teaser and a parlay?

Both require every leg to win, but a teaser lets you move the spread or total on each leg in your favor first, in exchange for lower payout odds than a standard parlay of the same size would offer.

Do all sportsbooks offer the same 6-point teaser odds?

No. Payout odds for the same size and point value of teaser can vary meaningfully between operators, and some books adjust pricing specifically on teasers that fall into the classic Wong range, so it's worth comparing before betting.

Can you tease a total instead of just a point spread?

Yes, most sportsbooks let you mix spreads and totals on the same teaser ticket. The same key-number logic applies less predictably to totals, though, since final combined scores don't cluster around one number as tightly as margins cluster around 3 and 7.

Why don't sharp bettors rely on teasers as heavily as parlays get discussed?

The theoretical edge in a well-constructed Wong teaser is real but historically thin, and sportsbooks have priced and restricted the bet accordingly over time. It's a legitimate strategy, not a reliable long-term profit source on its own.

Is a bigger teaser (more points) always a better trade?

No. A 10 or 13-point teaser crosses more numbers but costs far more in payout odds, and beyond a certain point you're buying protection you don't need on a game that was never close to those key numbers to begin with.
